Day 25: Rule 86

"If it exists, it can play Bad Apple"

It already exists for the SNES, but not the SNES CD / Nintendo PlayStation. I want to test my new CD development tools and opted to make this as a quick way to test them, as well as my custom BIOS. My version runs at 30 FPS with ease while the existing version caps at 20 FPS. It took a while to fine tune the converter, but now I have a basic MSU-1 build that can run on emulator and SD2SNES / FXPak. Next step is getting it to run off CD-ROM at 1x speed, which will be a little more trickier than MSU-1.

Here it is running on my SD2SNES. On a CRT the stars' and petals' pixels bleed into other pixels a little making colorful shimmers, but sadly my camera doesn't pick it up well.

Day 23: My raycast engine on SNES!

The raycast engine running on my SNES via SD2SNES Flashcart. Seeing it working on actual hardware feels really special, especially at a decent framerate. I used the 2.68 MHz SlowROM cartridge since the Nintendo PlayStation RAM most likely can only read at that speed, and I wanted to make sure the engine could work at an acceptable framerate for the original prototype.

It runs at sub 30 FPS framerates which might not be suitable for modern audiences, but that's where my BIOS adding the SuperFX chip that Nintendo and Sony planned on including comes in. In the future, when you run my game on the new BIOS, it will detect SuperFX compatibility and swap to code that fully takes advantage of the co-processor and deliver greatly improved framerates.

Day 22: Changing 'palette' with Texels

One other benefit of texel manipulation is having a cheap way to select a 'palette' despite the scene being rasterized to an 8bpp Mode 7 display area. With careful palette arrangement, it is possible for example to have vine covered stone walls & regular stone walls with just 1 texture, saving precious RAM space when the textures need to be stored there instead of ROM when the engine is moved to CD.

Day 21: Accidental Fog

I was reviewing the code for my raycasting engine and looking at what would be needed to port it to CD, and I came up with an idea of manipulating bits used for texels to save precious RAM space to create "dark side" textures without requiring a separate texture. A little more testing later, and I realized I could use this technique combined with distance from the player to create a fog effect that's cheap enough to work well on even a stock SNES.

I was originally planning on including some sort of dark room mechanic like Jurassic Park for the SNES, but I was thinking it would just make everything pitch black if you don't have an item that produces light. Now I can have a lot more control over lighting in the game based on environment and the player's equipment.

Day 20: First major milestone reached!

One of the major milestones for the SNES CD project was to make a build of SD2SNES that could run Nintendo PlayStation / SNES CD BIOS cartridges, and after a bunch of trial and error (and getting the IDE to build the firmware to work in the first place!) I was able to get it working on a real SNES! I can now test my new assembler for CD-based SNES games on this. This has always been important to me as I wanted to ensure my future CD games could run on existing SNES hardware, and existing emulators with MSU-1 support should be able to easily extend support for mapper and be able to play CD games with a MSU-1 build without issue.

Day 17: Super Assembler, the all-in-one SNES assembler!

One thing I found myself wanting when developing my SNES CD programs was a 65816 assembler that could also assemble SPC-700 and SuperFX programs, particularly one with syntax similar to the CA65 assembler which I am familiar with. I now have a brand assembler that does just that, with some refinements for the 65816 processor as CA65 was meant more for 6502 programs. And most importantly, it is capable of compiling SNES programs into CD and MSU-1 files ready to be run from my new BIOS ROM.

NATHANIEL HARRIS November 1, 2026 · 11:34 pmEST

Day 11: Reinventing the Font

Something I hadn't yet set up but needs to be done: displaying text. An easy task, but first I needed to make some graphics for them. I've made a couple variations, a blocky style like in old 8-bit systems, and a more natural look. There's a couple ways to go about displaying text on old tile-based hardware. Either you make every character in a font its own tile and take up a fixed size, in this case 8x8 pixels, or you rasterize text to tiles which you need to do if you want variable width font and kerning. For now, I'm going with simple tile based text.

About

I am Nathaniel Harris, a systems software engineer. I build reliable software for complex systems.

I am self-taught, and I have done this work for more than fifteen years, from custom voxel game engines to space-domain awareness tools. Most recently I worked on Forerunner at Space Interactions, on the services and pipelines behind satellite and orbital data, and the views that show it.

I work at every layer: Rust and MongoDB services, TypeScript and Electron frontends, C++ and HLSL on the GPU, and assembly on the bare machine. I learned all of it by hand, years before AI coding tools. Now I use agents like Claude Code to move faster, and fifteen years of doing the work myself is how I know when their output is right. I do my best work on small teams that build systems which seem impossible at that size.

I like domains where the rules are external and non-negotiable, such as orbital data, field-service operations and SMS compliance. To learn an unfamiliar system, I take it apart until its opinions become obvious. Then I work inside it, not against it.

Based in Interlochen, Michigan. Co-founder of Harris XR.
